articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than culverts. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.3 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 12 of 89 planned drainage projects
Public records show $8.2 million went to engineering consultants while $4.1 million funded actual construction
County staff turnover and a 2024 reorganization left the stormwater division without a permanent director for 14 months
articles.body:
The drainage ditch behind Marcus Wheeler's house on Doris Drive hasn't been cleared since 2019. He knows because he marks the date on his calendar every time a county truck shows up.

"They came once in seven years," Wheeler said, standing in his backyard where a foot of standing water had pooled three days after a May thunderstorm. "I've been paying this fee for three years now. Where's it going?"

The answer, according to 1,400 pages of public records obtained by The Flightline, is complicated. But the short version: mostly to studies, plans and consultants.

The Promise

In November 2022, Escambia County voters approved a stormwater utility fee by a margin of 58 to 42 percent. The ballot language promised "dedicated funding for drainage improvements, flood mitigation, and water quality protection." Residential property owners would pay $7 per month. Commercial rates varied by impervious surface area.

County Administrator Wes Moreno called it "a game-changer" at the December 2022 commission meeting. The fee would generate roughly $15 million annually. Staff presented a prioritized list of 89 projects, from culvert replacements to retention pond construction. The worst flooding areas—Brownsville, Brent, Myrtle Grove—would see work first.

Three and a half years later, the county has collected $47.3 million. It has completed 12 projects.

Where the Money Went

The Flightline filed public records requests for all stormwater fund expenditures from January 2023 through April 2026. The documents reveal a pattern: study after study, contract after contract, while construction lagged.

Engineering and consulting fees account for $8.2 million of the spending. The largest recipient is Jacobs Engineering, which holds a $3.4 million master services agreement for "stormwater program support." CDM Smith received $2.1 million for basin modeling. Volkert Inc. billed $1.8 million for design work on projects that have not broken ground.

Actual construction spending totals $4.1 million. The completed projects include six culvert replacements, four ditch improvements, and two outfall repairs. Average cost: $342,000 each.

Personnel costs absorbed $6.8 million. Equipment and materials accounted for $3.2 million. The remaining $25 million sits in reserve, according to the county's April 2026 financial report.

"You can't build anything without engineering first," said County Engineer Matt Langley at the May 14 commission meeting. "We're following the proper process."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh pressed back. "Three years of process and we've got $25 million in the bank while people's yards are flooding. At what point do we actually start building things?"

The Staffing Problem

Part of the delay traces to a reorganization that nobody asked for.

In March 2024, then-County Administrator Amy Lovoy merged the stormwater division with the roads department. The stormwater director position was eliminated. The previous director, Carlos Mendez, took a job with Santa Rosa County two weeks later.

For the next 14 months, stormwater operations reported to the roads superintendent, who also managed 847 miles of county roads, 12 bridges, and a $34 million paving program. Meeting minutes show stormwater items rarely made the agenda.

"We lost institutional knowledge," said a current Public Works employee who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. "Carlos knew every ditch in this county. The consultants are still trying to figure out what he already knew."

The county hired a new stormwater manager in May 2025. Jamie Thornton came from Hillsborough County, where she oversaw a $90 million annual stormwater program. She inherited a backlog of 77 unfinished projects, a half-completed basin study, and three consultant contracts with overlapping scopes of work.

"I'm not going to sugarcoat it," Thornton told commissioners in January 2026. "We're behind. But we have a plan to catch up."

The Plan to Catch Up

Thornton's 18-month acceleration plan calls for bidding 15 construction projects by December 2026. She consolidated the consultant contracts and brought some design work in-house. The April update showed four projects in active bidding.

But the timeline keeps slipping. A culvert replacement on West Navy Boulevard was supposed to bid in February. Permit issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection pushed it to June. A retention pond project in Bellview stalled when soil testing revealed contamination from a former dry cleaner. Remediation could add 18 months.

Meanwhile, the flooding continues. The National Weather Service recorded 67 inches of rain in Pensacola in 2025, about 5 inches above the annual average. May 2026 has already seen 8 inches.

Marcus Wheeler on Doris Drive isn't holding his breath. His neighborhood drainage project sits at number 43 on the county's priority list. At the current pace, he estimates work might start around 2031.

"I'll probably be dead by then," said Wheeler, who is 71. "Maybe my kids can enjoy a dry backyard."

What Happens Next

The Board of County Commissioners will review the stormwater program at its June 5 meeting. Commissioner Steven Barry has requested a "comprehensive accounting" of all fee revenue and expenditures. Commissioner Bergosh wants to see the consultant contracts rebid.

County Administrator Moreno—still in the job despite two rounds of commission turnover—defended the program's trajectory in a written statement to The Flightline.

"Stormwater infrastructure is complex and requires careful planning," he wrote. "The engineering work completed over the past three years positions us to accelerate construction. Residents will see significant progress in 2026 and 2027."

The 89-project list from 2022 has grown to 127 projects. Estimated total cost: $312 million. At current collection rates and spending pace, full buildout would take until 2047.

The fee was sold as a solution. Three years in, it looks more like a down payment on a problem that keeps getting bigger.

articles.label: Neighborhood
articles.headline: The Last Block of Belmont-DeVilliers
articles.dek: A single block on West Belmont Street holds four vacant lots, two shuttered businesses, and one 89-year-old woman who remembers when it was the center of Black Pensacola. Developers are circling.
brief: Dorothy Mae Henderson, 89, is the last original resident on the 400 block of West Belmont Street, once the commercial heart of Pensacola's historic Black business district.
Four vacant lots and two shuttered storefronts now surround her home, as developers have submitted three separate rezoning applications for the block since January.
Community advocates and city officials are debating whether new investment will revitalize the neighborhood or erase what remains of its history.
articles.body:
Dorothy Mae Henderson waters her azaleas at 6:30 every morning. She has done this for 61 years, since she and her husband James bought the shotgun house at 412 West Belmont Street in 1965. The azaleas are the same ones her mother-in-law planted. The house is the same one where she raised four children. The neighborhood is not.

"Used to be I couldn't water these flowers without somebody stopping to talk," Henderson said, standing on her porch last Tuesday. "Mr. Charlie at the barbershop. Miss Ernestine going to open the cafe. Now I water my flowers and I don't see nobody."

The 400 block of West Belmont Street runs 300 feet between N and A streets, one block north of where Belmont meets DeVilliers. In 1960, this stretch held 14 businesses and 22 residences. Today it holds four vacant lots, two shuttered storefronts, three rental properties and Henderson's house. She is the last original owner on the block.

She may not be an owner much longer. Since January, developers have filed three separate rezoning applications with the City of Pensacola covering portions of her block. The applications would allow mixed-use construction up to four stories. Henderson has received five unsolicited purchase offers in the past eight months, according to letters she showed The Flightline. The highest was $285,000—more than 10 times the home's current assessed value of $27,400.

"They send me these letters like I'm supposed to be grateful," Henderson said. "Like they're doing me a favor."

What Was Here

The Belmont-DeVilliers district was Pensacola's primary Black commercial center from the 1920s through the late 1960s. Segregation meant Black residents built their own economy: grocery stores, dentists, tailors, nightclubs, hotels. The intersection of Belmont and DeVilliers was the hub.

Henderson's block sat just north of that intersection. Her memories map a vanished geography.

"Right there where that lot is, that was Johnson's Grocery," she said, pointing east. "Next to that was the shoe repair. Across the street was Miss Ernestine's cafe—she made the best smothered pork chops in Pensacola. Mr. Charlie's barbershop was on the corner. That man cut hair for 50 years."

The businesses began closing after desegregation, when Black customers gained access to white-owned stores downtown and in the suburbs. Urban renewal accelerated the decline. In the 1970s and 1980s, the city demolished blocks of Belmont-DeVilliers for road widening and public housing that was later itself demolished.

Escambia County property records show that seven of the 14 businesses on Henderson's block in 1960 were demolished between 1971 and 1989. The remaining structures deteriorated. Owners died. Heirs scattered. By 2010, only five buildings remained standing on the block. Today there are four.

Who Wants In

The three rezoning applications tell different stories about the block's future.

The first, filed in January by Belmont Street Partners LLC, covers two vacant lots on the block's east end. The LLC is registered to a Tallahassee address. Its managing member, according to state corporate filings, is Coastal Land Acquisitions Inc., a company that has purchased 17 properties in the Belmont-DeVilliers area since 2021.

The second application, filed in March by a local developer named Marcus Webb, covers a single lot adjacent to Henderson's property. Webb told The Flightline he plans to build workforce housing.

"This neighborhood needs investment, not more empty lots," Webb said. "I grew up five blocks from here. I'm not trying to erase anything. I'm trying to build something."

The third application, filed in April, comes from the Community Redevelopment Agency itself. It covers the two shuttered storefronts—a former convenience store and a former beauty salon—that the city acquired through tax lien foreclosure in 2019 and 2023.

John Hartley, the CRA's executive director, said the agency is exploring options for the properties.

"We're committed to development that honors the history of this district," Hartley said. "That's why we're going through the public process. We want community input."

The CRA has scheduled a community meeting for June 4 at the Fricker Community Center to discuss the properties. As of press time, 12 people had signed up to attend.

The History Problem

In 2019, the Pensacola City Council designated a 15-block area including Henderson's street as the Belmont-DeVilliers Historic District. The designation was intended to protect remaining structures and guide future development.

Seven years later, advocates say the designation has done little.

"The historic district has no teeth," said Jamaal Washington, president of the Belmont-DeVilliers Neighborhood Association. "There's no design review. There's no demolition delay. A developer can tear down a 100-year-old building and put up whatever they want as long as it meets code."

Washington pointed to two examples from the past three years: a 1920s commercial building on DeVilliers Street demolished in 2024 for a parking lot, and a row of shotgun houses on Belmont Street torn down in 2023 for a self-storage facility.

City spokesperson Maria Santos said the historic designation provides recognition but was never intended to prevent all demolition.

"The designation identifies the area's historical significance," Santos wrote in an email. "Property owners retain the right to develop their land within existing zoning and code requirements."

The Florida Trust for Historic Preservation has twice contacted the city about strengthening protections for the district. Both times, according to correspondence obtained through a public records request, city staff responded that no changes were planned.

What Henderson Wants

Henderson has no plans to sell. She said this plainly, without drama, while sitting in her living room surrounded by 61 years of accumulated life: family photographs, church programs, a curio cabinet full of figurines her late husband collected.

"Where am I supposed to go?" she said. "This is my home. These are my people. Even if they're gone, they're still here."

Her children have encouraged her to consider the offers. Her oldest son, James Jr., who lives in Atlanta, said he worries about his mother alone on a block with so many vacant lots.

"It's not safe like it used to be," James Henderson Jr. said by phone. "I want her taken care of. But I also understand what that house means to her. What that street means."

Henderson's daily routine has contracted over the years. She attends Greater Mount Lily Baptist Church on Sundays. Her granddaughter brings groceries on Wednesdays. A home health aide visits on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The rest of the time, she tends her azaleas, watches her stories, and waits for neighbors who no longer come.

On the morning of this interview, a white Mercedes SUV slowed in front of her house. The driver, a man in a polo shirt, took photographs through the window. Henderson watched from her porch. She did not wave. The Mercedes drove on.

"They've been doing that for months," she said. "Taking pictures like I'm already gone."

The azaleas are blooming late this year. Henderson blames the mild winter. She expects they'll peak in another week or two, bright pink against the gray clapboard siding. She'll water them every morning until then. She'll water them every morning after.

"Sixty-one years," she said. "That's longer than most of these developers been alive. They think they know what this neighborhood needs. They don't know nothing about this neighborhood. They just know what it's worth."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Begins With a Hiring Crisis at NAS Pensacola
articles.dek: The base needs 200 seasonal workers for next week's air show. It has 61. What happened to the usual pipeline.
brief: NAS Pensacola has filled only 61 of 200 seasonal positions needed for next week's Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show
Base officials cite new federal background check requirements and competition from higher-paying private sector jobs
Commanders are reassigning active duty personnel to fill gaps in parking, crowd control and concessions
articles.body:
The parking lot at Sherman Field sits empty on a Thursday morning. In six days it will hold 150,000 people. Right now it holds Petty Officer Second Class Marcus Webb, walking the asphalt with a clipboard and a problem.

"We usually have a full crew by now," Webb said. "Trained, badged, ready to go. This year we're pulling sailors off desk duty."

NAS Pensacola needs 200 seasonal workers to run the Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show, the base's largest annual public event. As of Thursday morning, 61 positions have been filled. The rest remain vacant with eight days until gates open.

Base spokesman Lt. Commander Patricia Reyes confirmed the numbers but declined to characterize the situation as a crisis. "We are adapting our staffing model to meet current conditions," she said in a written statement. "The show will go on as planned."

New Rules, Old Pipeline

For two decades the hiring worked the same way. Escambia County schools let out in mid-May. Teenagers and college students home for summer applied for $12-an-hour jobs directing traffic, selling hot dogs, checking bags. The base ran background checks. Most cleared within 48 hours.

That pipeline broke in February.

New Department of Defense regulations implemented this year require all temporary civilian workers on military installations to complete an expanded background investigation through the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency. The process takes four to six weeks minimum. For applicants under 21 with limited credit and employment history, it often takes longer.

"We started posting positions in March," said Angela Torres, civilian human resources director for NAS Pensacola. "The first batch of clearances came back last week. We're still waiting on 89 more."

Of those 89 pending applications, Torres said 34 have withdrawn to take other jobs. Another 12 aged out of the seasonal employment window. The rest remain in bureaucratic limbo.

The Competition

The base pays seasonal workers $14.50 an hour, up from $12 two years ago. That raise came after a 2024 hiring shortfall forced last-minute scrambling.

It wasn't enough.

Amazon's Pensacola fulfillment center starts warehouse workers at $18. The new Whataburger on Navy Boulevard advertises $16 for counter staff. Flora-Bama, 20 miles west on Perdido Key, posts signs offering $20 plus tips for barbacks during the summer rush.

"My son applied to work the air show," said Cantonment resident Denise Holloway, waiting outside the base commissary Thursday. "By the time the background check came through, he'd already been at Publix for three weeks. They hired him in two days."

Torres acknowledged the wage gap but said federal pay scales limit what the base can offer. "We're constrained by GS and WG rate tables," she said. "A seasonal parking attendant in Pensacola gets the same rate as one in San Diego."

The Workaround

With the hiring shortfall now unavoidable, base commanders have activated a contingency plan that shifts the burden to active duty personnel.

An internal memo obtained by The Flightline shows 94 sailors and Marines from non-essential administrative roles have been reassigned to air show support duty. They will work parking, crowd control, shuttle buses and vendor assistance from May 28 through May 31.

"This is not ideal," said one Navy chief who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss staffing decisions. "These are people with actual jobs. Aviation maintenance. Supply. Admin. We're pulling them off their work to park cars."

The reassignments will not affect flight operations or the Blue Angels demonstration itself, according to Lt. Commander Reyes. "Operational readiness remains our priority," she said.

The Show Goes On

Blue Angels Homecoming draws visitors from across the Southeast. Hotels in downtown Pensacola and along Pensacola Beach report near-full bookings for the weekend. The Escambia County Tourist Development Council estimates the event generates $24 million in economic impact.

That figure does not account for secondary spending at restaurants, gas stations and rental properties throughout the week. Nor does it measure the less tangible value of the air show as Pensacola's signature civic event, a tradition stretching back to 1946.

"People come home for this," said Gulf Breeze resident Tom Nakamura, a retired Navy pilot who flew with the Blue Angels in the 1990s. "It's bigger than Memorial Day. Bigger than the Fair. This is what Pensacola is."

Whether the scaled-back civilian workforce will diminish the visitor experience remains to be seen. Base officials say they have contingency plans for longer wait times at parking lots and entry gates. Concession menus may be reduced. Some amenity tents will close early.

On Thursday morning, Marcus Webb finished his walk across Sherman Field. The asphalt was hot already at 9 a.m. By next Thursday it would be covered with lawn chairs, coolers, sunburned shoulders.

"We'll figure it out," he said. "That's what we do."

Applications for seasonal positions remain open through Monday. Information is available at the NAS Pensacola civilian employment office or at navyjobs.gov.
